title: Misinformation and professional news on largely unmoderated platforms: the case of telegram
screen_reason: Behavioural platform-data study of 202,571 Telegram channel posts containing links to two curated domain lists (94 misleading sources, 14 professional news sources). Table 1 reports the share of those link posts that pointed to misleading sources (76,056 = 38%), i.e. a quantitative share with a stated denominator for links carrying misinformation on a platform.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language public Telegram channels, US-focused source lists
estimates.measure_type: % of Telegram channel posts linking to a listed news source whose link went to a known misleading source (rather than a professional news source)
estimates.denominator: 202,571 Telegram channel posts (Oct 2018-Sep 2019) that contained a hyperlink to one of the 94 misleading or 14 professional news domains studied; these were only ~3% of the 6.8 million link-containing messages
estimates.definition: The post contained a hyperlink to a domain on the curated list of 94 misleading sources (Pierri et al. 2020 list, humor/parody sites removed by the authors)
estimates.misinfo_def: misleading sources are defined as ones that contain "misleading content, false and/or hyper-partisan news as well as hoaxes, conspiracy theories, click-bait and satire"
estimates.source_quote: Table 1. Descriptive statistics. Posts Views Shares Channel participants Professional News 126,515(62%) Mean 180.55 0.02 7,701 Misleading 76,056(38%) SD 1,729 0.19 35,753 Total 202,571
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pre-existing curated domain lists also used by Pierri et al. (2020), maintained since 2016 and used in Grinberg et al. (2019) and Shao et al. (2018); 94 misleading domains after the authors removed humor/parody sites; professional list = 14 'US most trusted news sources' from Pew (Mitchell et al. 2014). No inter-coder reliability applicable (list-based).
estimates.moderator_quote: For our analysis, we extracted all messages that contained hyperlinks to any website, which was 6.8 million messages. ... For the lists of professional news and misleading sources, we relied on curated lists also used by Pierri and colleagues (2020). ... This resulted in a list of 94 misleading sources (Claim Sources, 2020).
estimates.notes: Construct judgement: the unit counted is a channel post carrying a link, i.e. an act of dissemination, so coded SHARING/content_share per the rule that '% of shared links unreliable' is SHARING; a CONTENT reading (posts that exist on the platform) is defensible, hence borderline=true. The denominator is heavily curated: it contains ONLY posts linking to the 108 listed US domains, so 38% is not the prevalence of misinformation among all Telegram posts or all links. Data span two years (Oct 2018-Sep 2019); year coded 2019 (end of window). Caveat for adjudication: the appended misleading-source list still contains satire domains (theonion.com, babylonbee.com, duffelblog.com) and hyper-partisan-but-not-false outlets (dailycaller.com, redstate.com, rawstory.com, crooksandliars.com), so the numerator is 'unreliable/hyper-partisan source', much broader than false content.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) A prevalence-style figure is DERIVABLE but not stated: 76,056 misleading-source posts out of the '6.8 million' messages containing hyperlinks = ~1.1% of all link-containing Telegram posts. Not extracted because the denominator is stated only as a two-significant-figure rounding ('6.8 million'), which R8 excludes; flagged here because it is arguably the paper's most policy-relevant prevalence number. (2) 'Only 3% of the posts with hyperlinks in them contained links to either the professional news or misleading sources' - a share of link posts covered by BOTH lists combined, not a misinformation share, so no row. (3) Table 4 gives distinct channel counts (professional 1,258 vs misleading 435 channels; 100.57 vs 174.84 posts per channel). The paper's headline claim is concentration ('the audience for misinformation is not a general one, but a small and active community of users'), but no top-X%-of-users/sources -> Y%-of-exposure figure is reported, so R1 is not satisfiable and no CONCENTRATION row was created. (4) Mean views per post (professional 180.55, misleading 1,729) and regression coefficients (misleading posts 14% fewer views, 4.17x more likely to be shared, channels 18-34% more active) are effect sizes/means, not shares with denominators. (5) Appendices A1/A2 list per-domain URL counts but no shares.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of an open-access Telegram corpus (317m messages, 28,000 public channels, 2015-2019) built by snowball crawling from 250 English-language seed channels - explicitly non-random and non-comprehensive; authors restricted to Oct 2018-Sep 2019 (24.7m messages, 6.8m with links), dropped shortened URLs (~7% of links), and classified links against two pre-existing curated domain lists; no human coding and therefore no inter-coder reliability reported; regressions use HC1 robust SEs with year/month/weekday fixed effects.
rob.item6_quote: Within this list, professional or mainstream sources were defined as reliable news that mentioned "factual, objective and credible information" (Pierri et al., 2020), while misleading sources are defined as ones that contain "misleading content, false and/or hyper-partisan news as well as hoaxes, conspiracy theories, click-bait and satire."
rob.item10_quote: Only 3% of the posts with hyperlinks in them contained links to either the professional news or misleading sources in our study: the majority linked to other websites, mostly in other languages such as Farsi, Russian and Arabic.
